lawyer:
Bivhas Chandra Biswas with NM Borhan for Probir Haider Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
Abdul Quayum with Taposh Kumar Biswas and Md Selim Reza Chowdhury Advocates -----For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Kamakshya Ranjan Haider and ors ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Prafullya Kumar Haider & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Plaintiffs obtained this Rule from a judgment of reversal. They instituted title suit No. 76 of 1995 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Nazirpur, Pirojpur seeking declaration of title in respect of 1.84 acres of land as described in schedule Ga to the plaint. In course of hearing of the Rule, they filed an application for amendment of the plaint seeking addition of a relief for partition and allotment of saham of 1.84 acres of land. The application was allowed by a separate order. The suit is now for partition on declaring the plaintiffs' title in respect of 1.84 acres of land.

2. Plaintiffs' case, in short is, that the suit lands along with other lands appertained to RS khatian No. 21 measuring an area of 12.95 acres belonged to Rajmohon, Ketu and Panchu. Rajmohon had 4.27 acres of land in his share and on his death, his 8 sons Kailash, Rasik, Rojoni, Surjokanto, Rakhal, Piyari and Choto inherited their respective shares. Ketu died unmarried while he was jointly residing with his brother Rajmohon leaving wife Feli and nephew Kailash Chandra. During his lifetime Ketu executed a registered will in respect of his share of land giving 12 annas share to Kailash Chandra and 4 annas share to his wife Feli, specifically pointing out that on her demise Kailash would inherit the entire lands. Accordingly, after the death of Feli, Kailash got Ketu's share of 4.27 acres and inherited 0.59 acres as son of Rajmohan. Jogesh Chandra being the only son of Kailash inherited the said lands but in the RS khatian 4 annas share was wrongly recorded in his name though he had 6 annas share. Panchu died leaving two sons, Kanai Lal and Kalicharan @ Khoka but in the RS and SA khatians more shares than they were legally entitled to were recorded in their names. Jogesh Chandra transferred 1.34 acres of land out of his 4.86 acres by registered kabala dated 19th August 1957 in favour of the plaintiff No. 1, his mother Maloti and the plaintiff No. 4. On the same day, Jogesh also transferred 1.34 acres of land by another deed in favour of the plaintiffs-predecessors Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish. Kalicharan @ Khoka exchanged 0.84 acres of land by a registered deed dated 2nd June 1958 with plaintiffs-predecessors Mohananda, Kaishore and Satish out of his inherited property and in pursuance of that exchange, the plaintiffs-predecessors got lands in Shakhari Kati mouja and Kalicharan got lands in the suit Gaokhali mouja. Mohananda died leaving no issue and accordingly Kaishore inherited his share and on the death of Kaishore, the plaintiffs Nos. 1-3 got his share. Satish also died leaving no issue while residing jointly with his sister Maloti and accordingly, the plaintiffs Nos. 1-3 got his share as well. In this way the plaintiffs are claiming title in respect of 1.84 acres of land.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. According to them, in the suit khatian Rajmohon, Ketu and Panchu had 13.13 acres of land and accordingly, each brother had 4.38 acres of land. Rajmohon died leaving 8 sons and each son inherited 0.49½ acres of land. Ketu died leaving no issue and therefore, his brother Panchu Ram inherited his share. In the premises, Panchu had 8.75 acres of land from his share and as reversionary heir of Ketu. Out of 13.13 acres of land, 1.16 acres were settled to the tenants and therefore, Rajmohon, Panchu and Ketu had  11.79 acres of land and accordingly, Panchu Ram in fact had 7.86 acres and after his death, Kanai and Kalicharan, his two sons, inherited the lands. Kanai died leaving 4 sons, Judhusthir, Nittyananda, Gouranga and Narayan. They by 5 registered deeds transferred 3.93 acres of land in favour of defendant No. 3. They claimed that although the RS record was incorrect but their title was not clouded and that the deed of exchange was forged, collusive and the plaintiffs did not acquire any title on the basis of those deeds.

4. Plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses and exhibited series of documentary evidence in support of their claim in the suit lands. The defendants also examined 4 witnesses and filed some documentary evidence in support of their claim. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit in part declaring plaintiffs' title in respect of 1.39-1/3 acres of land. The defendants preferred title appeal No. 91 of 2000 from the said judgment and decree. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Pirojpur by judgment and order dated 11th October, 2002 allowed the appeal and set aside those of the trial Court.

5. Admittedly, the petitioners are the co-sharers in the suit khatian. According to the plaintiffs, they have title in respect of 1.84 acres of land in the suit khatian as described in schedule 'ga' to the plaint. On the other hand, the defendant admitted that the plaintiffs are entitled to only 0.49½ acres of land as their predecessor Kailash did not get the share of Ketu and that Ketu's brother Panchu, the defendants' predecessor, inherited his share. Therefore, the main controversy in this suit is, who has inherited share of Ketu? The learned Joint District Judge observed that the record of 4(four) annas share in RS khatian No. 21 (Exhibit 1) in Kailash's name proved that besides inheritance, Kailash got lands from other source and as a result, the RS khatian was prepared. He further observed that the RS khatian did not prove that Kanai and Kalicharan, sons of Panchu, inherited 7.86 acres of land from his father and from the share of Ketu, inasmuch as, in the said khatian Panchu's 1/3rd share was recorded in their names that proved that Punchu did not get Ketu's share. The trial Court further held that plaintiffs' predecessors purchased 2.68 acres of land out of 4.86 acres by two deeds dated 19th August, 1957 (Exhibits 4 and 5) from Jogesh, son of Kailash and after they exchanged 0.84 acres of land from the suit Mouja with Kalicharan, the plaintiffs had 1.84 acres of land in the suit khatian after excluding 0.84 acres, which is the disputed 'ga' schedule lands. By the deeds of exchange the plaintiffs predecessors got 0.84 acres of lands from Shakhari Kathi Mouja and Kalicharan got 0.84 acres of land from the suit Mouja (Exhibits 6 and 6(ka). He further held that Exhibit 2 indicated that Mohananda, Lalit, Adityo and Dwijabor, were sons of Jagabandhu Haider that proved that Mohananda had three full brothers, and thus, in presence of full brothers, Kaishore being the cousin of Mohananda did not inherit Mahananda's share. In view of the above, the trial Court came to the conclusion that Mohamanda had 0.4475 acres of land out of 1.34 acres he along with his brothers acquired by purchase jointly by kabala dated 19th August 1957 (Exhibit 5) from Jogesh, that as the plaintiffs failed to prove that they inherited the share of Mohananda, they were entitled to 2.2325 acres after deducting 0.4475 acres of Mohananda's share, and that out of that lands their predecessors Kaishsore, Mohananda and Satish exchanged 0.84 acres of land with Kalicharan on 10th June 1958, (Exhibit 6(ka)) and thus, they have title in respect of 1.3925 (2.2325-0.84) acres of land in schedule 'ga'.

6. The trial Court further held that on the death of Panchu his two sons Kanai and Kalicharan inherited 2.135 acres each and on the death of Kanai, his sons Judisthir, Nittyananda, Gouranga and Narayan acquired title of 2.135 acres and not 3.93 acres, that the defendant No. 3 failed to produce title deeds that his predecessors Judisthir, Nittananda, Gouranga and Narayan had title in respect of 3.93 acres of land, that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 being the heirs of Kalicharan inherited 2.135 acres of land and therefore, they are entitled to 2.135 acres of land and that the RS khatian proved that Panchu's sons, Kanailal and Kalicharan have inherited his 1/3rd share.

7. The lower appellate Court observed that in the remark column of RS khatian only 0.70 acres of land was shown in the possession of Kailash and other co-sharers were in possession of other plots, that on the basis of such possession 7.96 acres of land was recorded in the corresponding SA Khatian No. 39, in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan, and 0.70 acres of land in the name of Jogesh in khatian No. 213 and that these khatians proved that despite mentioning 4 annas share in the khatian Kailash was in possession of only 0.70 acres of land. These findings of the Court of appeal below are based upon hypothesis, inasmuch as if Kailash did not get the share of Ketu on the basis of will, there was no reason for recording /4/ annas share in his name in Exhibit-1. His share in the lands of RS khatian would have been equal with his other seven brothers. The Court of appeal below without assigning any reason observed that Kailash was not in possession on the basis of the record which finding is in conflict with earlier finding. The Court of appeal below also did not reverse the findings of the trial Court that this recording in the khatian proved that Kailash got other lands apart from his father Rajmohan. Plaintiffs claimed that this record of /4/ annas share was due to mistake but, in fact, he was entitled to /6/ annas share on the basis of the registered deed of will dated 17th February, 1913 (Exhibit-7).

8. In the RS khatian (Exhibit 1) 3 annas and odd i.e. 1/3rd share, was recorded in the names of Kanai and Kalicharan, the predecessors of the defendants. The trial Court on consideration of this khatian, rightly held that the RS record did not support the claim of the defendants that Panchu inherited the share of Ketu and that after the death of Panchu, his sons Kanailal and Kalicharan did not inherit the share of Panchu. The lower appellate Court did not at all consider these findings of the trial Court and on a superficial consideration of the khatians held that the RS khatian supported the defendants' claim. The Court of appeal below failed to consider that the defendants had knowledge about the recording of /4/ share in the name of Kailash but their explanation was that despite such record, their title was not clouded; they however, failed to substantiate their claim. They have not challenged the RS khatian at any point of time which has presumptive value.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate, fails to explain the basis of recording /4/ annas share in the name of Kailash and the basis for recording 7.96 acres of laud in the SA khatian in the name of defendants' predecessors. Learned Advocate, however, contends that though in the RS khatian less share has been recorded in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan than they were legally entitled to, the SA khatian has been correctly prepared as they have inherited Ketu's share. This submission of the learned Advocate is the reiteration of the defendants' claim but the defendants have adduced no legal evidence in support of their claim, other than the SA khatian, The recitals in the will disprove their claim.

10. The Court of appeal below disbelieved the plaintiffs' claim on the reasonings that though in the will Kektu's name was mentioned but no schedule of the land was mentioned in it, that the plaintiffs did not prove the signatures of Ketu Rain and the attesting witnesses, and the contents of the will in accordance with law, that the plaintiffs did not mention the will in the plaint but later on they incorporated the story of will by way of amendment, that there is no evidence to show that Ketu Ram died before the Succession Act, 1925 came into force and that as the will was not probated, it was not acted upon and therefore, Kailash did not inherit Ketu's share of 4.27 acres of land. These findings of the Court of appeal below are not only self-contra-dictory but also based upon misconception of law.

<u>11. An amendment in the plaint is allowed for determining the real question in controversy between the parties and once an amendment of the plaint is allowed the amendment will relate back to the date of the institution of the suit and will be operative from that date. The defendants did not challenge the amendment in the plaint and the Court of appeal below, in the premises, erred in law in disputing the plaintiffs' claim only because those facts were not pleaded in the original plaint. The Court of appeal below fell in an error in failing to appreciate that no particular form is necessary in executing a will. It is sufficient if it contains the testamentary wishes of the deceased; the reference in this connection is sections 377 and 378 of the Hindu Law. A will is the legal declaration of the intention of a testator with respect to his property which he desires to be carried into effect after his death. Primarily, the words of the will are to be considered. They convey the expression of the stator's wishes. In Exhibit 7 the testator stated that on his demise, his wife Feli and nephew Kailash would enjoy his property in /4/ and /12/ annas share respectively and that on the death of his wife, Kailash would get her share as well. It is a registered instrument and executed on 17th February, 1913, more than 86 years prior to its filing in Court on 23rd November, 1999 by the plaintiffs from their custody claiming that Kailash got Ketu's share in the khatian on the strength of this will. It being a document of more than 30 years old produced from the proper custody, the Court may presume that (a) the signature and every other part of it which purports to be in the handwriting of the scribe is in that person's' handwriting, (b) the will was executed by Ketu, and (c) the will was attested by the persons by whom it purported to have been attested under section 90 of the Evidence Act. There is also presumption that the will was prepared at the time it was purported to have been prepared. The Court of appeal below has totally ignored this legal aspect of the matter while considering the will, Exhibit 7.</u>

12. The finding of the Court of appeal below that this will has not been acted upon in the absence of the probate of the will is also based upon misconception of law. Apart from the legal position, there are sufficient documentary evidence on record suggesting that this will has been acted upon. In the RS khatiar (Exhibit 1) 4 annas share was recorded in the name of Kailash and if the will had not been acted upon, his share would have been shown equal with his other brothers. Exhibit-6 proved that Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish exchanged 0.84 acres of land by registered deed of exchange with Kalicharan alias Khoka, son of Panchu out of 1.34 acres of land which they purchased from Jogesh son of Kailash by registered kabala dated 19th August 1957 (Exhibit 5). By this deed of exchange (Exhibit 6) Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish got lands from Shakhari Kati Mouja and Kali Charan got lands from the suit Mouja Goakhali (Exhibit 6(ka)). Kalicharan, the predecessor of the defendants acknowledged the title of Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish, who had got those lands from Jogesh. Kailash inherited only 0.59 acres from the share of Rajmohan according to the plaintiffs, and according to the defendants. he inherited only 0.49-1/3 acres bu this son Jogesh had transferred 1.34 acres of land by Exhibit 5 out of the suit khatian. Therefore, unless the deeds, Exhibits 5 and 7, were acted upon, Kalicharan would not have exchanged lands. Therefore, there is no doubt that the will was acted upon, and the defendants predecessor had acknowledged the acquiring of Kailash's title on the strength of the will, and that these deeds of will and exchange being old registered instruments have presumptive value in the absence of contrary evidence.

13. The Court of appeal below misread the RS khatian and observed that the RS khatian No. 21 and SA khatian No. 39 (Exhibit Kha and Kha(1)) proved that 7.96 acres of land were recorded in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan, sons of Panchu Rain. In RS khatian (Exhibit Kha) which corresponds to Exhibit-1, only 3 annas and odd share has been recorded in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan. In the SA Khatian 7.96 acres of lands were recorded in their names but in view of the above findings I find no basis of this record. There is no presumptive value of SA Khatian and the defendants-opposite panties have failed to show the basis of recording lands as such. The Court of appeal below disbelieved the plaintiffs claim of transfer of 1.34 +1.34 acres of land by Jogesh by registered kabalas dated 19th August, 1957 (Exhibits 4 and 5) in favour of Kamakkha Ranjan, the plaintiff No. 1, Malati Rani, mother of plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and Laxmi Rani, the plaintiff No. 4, and Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish respectively on the reasonings that Exhibit 4 was a certified copy, which the deed was entered in Volume No. 2770, but they did not call for the original volume for reception of secondary evidence and that the dag, khatian numbers and the areas of the lands in these deeds were identical.

14. The Court of appeal below was of the view that the deeds were created by the predecessor of the plaintiffs Kaishore Chandra for which the original deed (Exhibit 4) was not produced. The Court of appeal below failed to notice that Exhibit 4 was admitted into evidence without any objection and out of 1.34 acres lands transferred by Jogesh in favour of Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish (Exhibit 5), Kalicharan got 0.84 acres by way of exchange from Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish (Exhibit 6 ka). The registration number of Exhibit 4 is 2776 and it was registered in registration book No. 1 at pages 13-15. It was executed by Jogesh in favour of Kamakkah, Maloti and Laxmi Rani. Whereas, Exhibit 5, is registered deed No. 2777 and the said deed was executed by Jogesh in favour of Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish. This deed was entered in registration book No. 1 at pages 16-19. These facts prove that these deeds have been executed simultaneously and that the recipients of these deeds are distinct persons, and also in respect of separate lands out of the total area of 12.95 acres in the khatian. Therefore, there is no doubt that by these deeds different lands have been transferred to different sets of persons out of the same plot. The Court of appeal below on a superficial consideration of these two deeds observed that these deeds were collusively created by Kaishore Chandra.

15. As observed above, Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish, jointly on one side, and Kalicharan on the other exchanged suit plots No. 2209, 2210 and 2213 of Mouja Gaokhali with the lands of mouja Shakharkati of plot Nos. 1557, 2040, 2005, 20089, 2234, 2204, 2205 and 2208 by executing two registered deeds. The Court of appeal below found fault in the deeds on the reasonings that the second parties in those deeds did not put their signatures and that Exhibit 6(ka) was a certified copy. The Court of appeal below failed to notice that the parties did not execute one deed of exchange, rather they executed two deeds and in their respective deeds they put their signatures. The deeds were very old instruments executed on 10th June 1958 and there was reference in Exhibit '6' about Exhibit 6(ka), the original of which was lying with the defendants predecessor as he was the recipients of the lands. In Exhibit 6(ka) Kalicharan acknowledged the title of Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish in respect of 0.84 acres of land of suit plots No. 2209, 2210 and 2213, who got the said lands from Jogesh by kabala dated 19th August, 1957 (Exhibit 5). The defendants simply said that this deed of exchange was collusive but they did not lead any evidence in support of their claim of collusion. This is a registered deed and this deed proved that the deed of will was acted upon and by dint of this will, Kailash got Ketu's share, and after his death, Jogeshinherited the same and thereafter, Jogesh transferred the same to Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish and thereafter, Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish exchanged three plots with Kalicharan. The lands of Shakharkati mouja have been recorded in RS khatian No. 17 (Exhibit 2). Since Khoka @ Kali-charan acknowledged the title of Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish, the Court of appeal below erred in law in holding that this deed of exchange was a collusive one.

16. The Court of appeal below on a misreading of the evidence on record disbelieved the plaintiffs' possession. In support of plaintiffs' possession, they examined 3 witnesses, of them, PW 1 Kamakkha Ranjan Haider stated that he along with other plaintiffs have been possessing 1.84 acres of land in RS khatian No. 21 excluding 0.84 acres of land and also other lands in RS khatian No. 17. In cross-examination, he said that they have been possessing 2.68 acres of land in plots No. 2208, 2209, 2210 and 2213. PW 2 Motaleb Bepari stated that he has been borga cultivating 0.74 acres of land in plot No. 2208, and 1.14 acres in plot No. 2209. The Court of appeal below observed that PW 2 did not corroborate the plaintiffs claim in the plaint. This witness deposed about the lands he was borga cultivating on behalf of the plaintiffs. He was not deposing on behalf of the plaintiffs in respect of their entire lands. The Court of appeal below also disbelieved PW 3 Abdul Latif Miah observing that though he deposed in support of plaintiffs' possession but in course of cross-examination he failed to say the boundary of the suit lands. The Court of appeal below misread his evidence. He stated in course of cross-examination that "মামলার জমির চৌহদ্দী বলতে পারব" He did not say that he could not say the boundary of the suit lands.

17. Apart from the oral evidence, the defendants also admitted the plaintiffs' title and possession at least in respect of 0.49-1/2 acres of land. They did not altogether deny the plaintiffs' title in the suit lands. The plaintiffs are admitted co-sharers in the khatian. Admittedly the suit lands remain in ejmali and in view of the observations of the appellate Court about the maintainability of the suit, the plaintiffs filed an application for amendment of the plaint seeking partition and the application was allowed.

18. Mr Quayum, learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite parties, while supporting the views of the Court of appeal below, submits that in view of section 213 of the Succession Act, 1925 which corresponds section 187 of Act of 1865, the executor or the legatee cannot claim a right in the properties of the testator unless Probate of the will or Letters of Administration in respect of the will has been obtained and proved. This contention of the learned Advocate is devoid of substance. After the Hindu Wills Act, 1870, came into force, a Hindu will is required to be in writing and signed by the testator and attested by two witnesses. No Probate or Letter of Administration is required to be granted in respect of will executed by a Hindu in respect of joint family property. Before passing of the Hindu Wills Act, the estate of the deceased Hindu did not vest in his executor even if a probate was granted to him; the executor became the legal representative of the testator. The grant of Probate or the Letter of Administration took effect only for the purpose of recovery of debts and securing debtors paying the same. This Act of 1870 incorporated section 179 of the Indian Succession Act, 1865 which provided:

"The executor or administrator, as the case may be, of a deceased person, is his legal representative for all purposes, and all the property of the deceased person vests in him as such."

19. Section 179 of the Succession Act, 1865 corresponds to section 211 of the Succession Act, 1925 and this section did not apply to an executor under the Hindu Will, before the Hindu Wills Act came into force. His position was analogous to that of the manager of a minor heir under the Hindu Law. The Probate and Administration Act altered the law and made this section inapplicable to Hindus by deleting section 179. Although section 4 of the Probate and Administration Act contained a provision similar to section 179 of Act of 1865, that section contained a proviso saving the rights of the members of a joint Hindu family. Under this provision the executor derives his title from the will, immediately upon the testator's death his property vests in the executor, for the law knows no interval between the testator's death and vesting of the property. The executor or administrator, by virtue of his office or, in other words, in the character of executor or administrator, takes an estate in the property of the deceased, and a legal character is vested in him. The executor derives his title from the will and not from the probate. Therefore, I find no force in the contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties.

20. The Indian Succession Act, 1865 is applicable in this case since the will was executed before the Succession Act 1925 came into force. The Hindu Wills Act applied to certain wills only being those in respect of (a) wills made by a Hindu on or after 1st day of September 1870 within the territories which at the said date were subject to the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal, (section 369(a) of the Hindu Law), and (b) to such wills made outside the territory so far as related to immovable property situated within that limit. The Hindu Wills Act did not apply to all Hindu wills. The Probate and Administration Act, 1881 applied to all Hindu wills. This Act repealed section 179 of the Indian Succession Act, 1865 as part of Hindu Wills Act, but reenacted it as part of itself in section 4. The Probate and Administrative Act and the Hindu Wills Act have been repealed and reenacted by the Indian Succession Act.

21. In Raja Rama vs Fakruddin Sahib 122 IC 504, though the will was executed by a Mohammedan, on consideration of the provisions of Succession Act and Williams of Executors, Vol-1, page 220, it was observed:

"the executor derives his title from the Will. Immediately upon the testator's death his property vests in the executor, for the law knows no interval between the testator's death and the vesting of the property. It follows that before and without obtaining Probate the executor may do most things which appertain to his office thus, he may take possession of the testator's property, he may pay, or take releases of debts owing from the estate; and he may receive or release debts which are owing to it. The grant of Probate does not give him his title: it makes his title certain."

22. In Kadiyala Venkata Subamma vs Katreddi Ramayya 136 IC, 111 (PC) corresponding to 59 IA 112, the will in question was executed by one Madduru Venkata Subanna, a Hindu, some time in 1916 appointing his widow as executrix but she did not obtain probate of the will. She alienated some properties to her adopted son and others. Some beneficiaries of the will instituted the suit to enforce their right to particular parcels of land claiming that shortly after the testator's death the same was allotted to their share or, in the alternative, they claimed partition of the estate on the allegation that the executrix had, in the absence of probate, no power to make, and which were further charged as fraudulent. The suit was decreed. A single Bench of the Madras High Court referred the matter to a Full Bench for deciding "whether an executor appointed by will made in mufassil of the presidency has vested in him the estate of the testator as set out in the Probate and Administration Act, even though such executor does not obtain probate of the will" The Full Bench took into consideration of different provisions of the Wills Act, the Probate and Administration Act, 1881, and sections 179 and 188 of the Succession Act 1865, and answered the point as under:

"In case of Hindu wills to which Hindu Wills Act does not apply, the estate vests in the executor from the date of testator's death and that the provisions of Probate and Administrative Act are applicable, even though probate has not been obtained."

The matter went to the Privy Council. Their Lordships took into consideration sections 4 and 90 of the Probate and Administration Act; which read:

Section 4—An executor or Administrator, as the case may be, of a deceased person is his legal representative for all purposes, and all the property of the deceased person vests in him as such."

"Section 90(1)—An executor or administrator has, subject to the provisions of this section, power to dispose, as he thinks fit, of all or any of the property for the time being vested in him under section 4."

"(2)—The power of an executor to dispose of immovable property so vested in him is subject to any restriction which may be imposed in this behalf by the will appointing him, unless probate has been granted to him, and the Court which granted the probate permits him by an order in writing, notwithstanding the restriction, to dispose of any immovable property specified in the Order in a manner permitted by the Order."

Their Lordships were of the view that the Hindu Wills Act had no application in the case and that greater part of the Probate and Administration Act applied to the will and observed as follows:

"Section 4 makes no reference to probate, nor does the definition of 'executor' in section 3 (again reproduction from the Act of 1865) suggest that probate is any part of his title; he is merely the person to whom the testator has confided the carrying out of his disposition.

"So, too, section 90(2) clearly conceives of an executor not clothed with probate being able to dispose of the property "vested in him under section 4". It makes such power subject to any restriction imposed by the Will "unless probate has been granted", in which case the Court may relieve him from the restriction. In view of the terms of this section their Lordships think it would be impossible to hold that before probate nothing vested in the executor, and that he had no power of disposal at all,"

<u>23. Mr Quayum has not cited any authority in support of his contention. The intention of section 213 of the Succession Act 1925 is that an executor or legatee cannot establish his right as executor or legatee in a Court without obtaining probate, but there is nothing to prevent the executor from dealing with the property of the testator without obtaining probate, because as per section 211 the executor is the legal representative of the testator for all purposes, and all property vest in him as such, so that the grant of probate is not a condition precedent to such acts.</u>

24. In the will in question (Exhibit 7), it was clearly recited by the testator that his brother Panch Kari Haider did not reside in his house and thus he was not entitled to get anything from his estate and that if Panch Kari had looked after his wife in his absence and if he had maintained cordial relationship with Kailash, the executor would in his discretion give him something from his estate. The defendants did not adduce any evidence that Panch Mari looked after Ketu's wife or that he maintained cordial relationship with Kailash and thus he had got some lands from the share of Ketu. The will was not a conditional one and no restriction seemed to have been imposed upon the executor. In the absence of any restriction in the management of the estate, the executor had acquired absolute discretion to manage the estate of the deceased and the will was effective after the death of the testator and Kailash got the share of Ketu. The principles of law stated by their Lordships of the Privy Council are very much applicable in this case. I find no cogent ground to depart from their Lordships' views.

25. The trial Court thoroughly considered Exhibits 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, (ka) and 7 and rightly held that the plaintiffs have acquired title in respect of 1.3925 acres of land in schedule 'Ga' property excluding 0.84 acres of land which they exchanged. The trial Court has rightly held that the plaintiffs have title in respect of 1.3925 acres of land in schedule 'gha' lands. The Court of appeal below did not reverse all the findings of the trial Court. It had superficially considered the evidence and dismissed the suit by making conflicting findings. In view of the above, I find that the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal, which is liable to be interfered with. The Court of appeal below has committed error of law in interfering with the judgment of the trial Court which has occasioned as failure of justice. There is merit in this Rule.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below is set aside and restored those of the trial Court subject to the modification that the plaintiffs are entitled to a saham of 1.3925 acres of land in schedule 'ga' to the plaint subject to payment of requisite court fees within one month of the date of receipt of the record. I direct the parties to amicably partition the lands within 60 days from the date of receipt of the record, failing which, the plaintiffs are entitled to get their saham allotted through Court by appointment of an Advocate Commissioner.

End.
